subject: Critical Thinking
title: Conspiracy Theories: A Fallacy Ecosystem
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Conspiracy Theories: A Fallacy Ecosystem.

hook.text: Every conspiracy theory is an interlocking web of fallacies — each one shielding the others from falsification.

buildup.text: They use circular reasoning (the cover-up proves the conspiracy), ad hominem (critics are shills), and unfalsifiability.

discovery.text: Evidence against the theory becomes evidence for it: 'They're hiding the truth!' This makes the theory immune to.

twist.text: Real conspiracies do exist – Watergate, Enron.

climax.text: The litmus test: 'What evidence would change your mind?' If nothing could, you're not reasoning — you're believing.

punchline.text: If no evidence can disprove it, it's not a theory. It's a faith.

quiz.question: What makes conspiracy theories resistant to debunking?
options: Evidence against them is reinterpreted as evidence for them

details.summary: Conspiracy theories are not single fallacies but ecosystems of many fallacies working together: unfalsifiability, ad hominem, cherry-picking, and circular reasoning all reinforce each other to create a self-sealing belief system.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding conspiracy theories as fallacy clusters explains why they resist individual debunking and why each refutation strengthens the theory rather than weakening it.
takeaways: Conspiracy theories combine multiple fallacies into a self-sealing system
Counterevidence is reinterpreted as proof of the conspiracy
Addressing the underlying psychological needs is more effective than refuting individual claims

faq.question: Why do conspiracy theories become stronger when contradicted by evidence?
faq.answer: The theory reinterprets contradicting evidence as planted by the conspirators, making opposition into confirmation. This self-sealing property means the theory can absorb any evidence, turning standard debunking into fuel.

faq.question: What psychological needs do conspiracy theories satisfy?
faq.answer: They provide causal explanations for distressing events, a sense of special knowledge and group belonging, and a feeling of control in a chaotic world. Addressing these needs is more effective than fact-checking alone.
